# The Freezer

My mother died in March and left behind a chest freezer full of soup.

I found it the second week, after the funeral casseroles had stopped arriving and I'd run out of excuses not to go through the house. It sat in the garage under a quilted cover she'd sewn for it, as if it were a birdcage or a sleeping animal. I lifted the lid expecting frost-burned peas and a turkey from some forgotten Thanksgiving. Instead: rows. Dozens of quart containers, stacked with the precision of a woman who had once alphabetized her spice rack and then, years later, re-alphabetized it by frequency of use.

Each lid had a strip of masking tape. Each strip had her handwriting.

*Split pea — Jan 2019 — snowed in, radio said 14".*

*Chicken & rice — Oct 2020 — D. called, sounds better.*

*Minestrone — Aug 2017 — too many zucchini again, never again (lie).*

I stood there with the cold pouring out over my shins and read them the way you'd read someone's diary if you were sure they'd never find out. D. was my brother. He had not sounded better in October 2020, not really, but I suppose she'd needed to write it down to make it so.

---

I should explain that my mother was not a sentimental person. She threw away birthday cards after a week. She said photographs were for people who didn't trust their memories, and she trusted hers completely, right up until the last year, when it began quietly abandoning her like a tenant slipping out before the rent was due. She kept no journal. When I asked her once, as a teenager, whether she'd ever been in love before my father, she said, "Of course," and went back to shelling beans, and that was the entire oral history.

So the labels undid me a little. Here was the record she swore she didn't keep, written in the one language she'd always been fluent in.

*Lentil — Mar 2016 — first robin. Knee bad.*

*Beef barley — Dec 2018 — made for Ruth, she won't eat it, froze rest.*

*Tomato — Sept 2021 — can't remember if I already made this year. Making anyway.*

That one I held for a long time.

---

I didn't know what to do with them. Throwing them out felt like burning letters. Giving them away felt worse, like letting strangers read the letters first. The freezer hummed along beside me, running up an electric bill for a dead woman, keeping her afternoons at zero degrees.

In the end, I decided to eat them.

Not all at once. One a week, maybe two. I took the oldest first, because that seemed like the proper order, the order she'd have wanted: first in, first out. *Vegetable — Feb 2015 — power out 2 days, cooked on the woodstove, tastes like smoke.* It did taste like smoke. It also tasted a bit like freezer, which after eight years was fair. I ate it at her kitchen table with the window open, and outside a cardinal kept flinging itself at its own reflection in the car mirror, and I thought, *She would have written that down.* So I did. I started a notebook.

---

This went on through spring. I learned things.

I learned she'd had a friend named Ruth who was dying slowly across most of 2018 and whom I had never heard of. I learned that the zucchini situation was a recurring crisis of her own making, which she acknowledged annually and addressed never. I learned that she listened to the Saturday opera broadcast on the radio, because three different labels mentioned what was on: *Tosca, too loud. Carmen. Something German, turned it off.* I learned the date my father's brother died, which I had known, and the date she stopped setting two places at the table, which I hadn't.

*Potato leek — Apr 2019 — one bowl.*

That was all it said. One bowl.

I learned, as the dates crept forward, what her decline looked like from the inside. The handwriting got larger. The notes got shorter. Some containers had two labels, the second one contradicting the first. One was marked only *soup* and the date, and it turned out to be applesauce, and I laughed out loud alone in her kitchen and then cried for twenty minutes, which is how most things went that spring.

---

By June there were four left.

I'd started rationing. I'd go a week, then two, without opening the freezer, telling myself I was busy, which I wasn't. It's a strange thing to be afraid of reaching the end of someone's soup. But every quart I ate was a quart she would never make again, and some stupid animal part of me believed that as long as there was one in the freezer, she was still, in some small refrigerated way, in progress.

My brother came up for a weekend in July. I told him about the labels. I thought he might find it morbid, or funny, or both. Instead he went quiet and asked if there were any left, and I said three, and he asked if he could have one.

We chose together. *Chicken & rice — Oct 2020 — D. called, sounds better.*

He read the label and didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "I wasn't better."

"I know," I said.

"She knew too."

"I know."

We heated it up and ate it on the back steps, passing the pot between us like teenagers with a bottle, and it was very good soup. It had a lot of pepper in it. She always said pepper was for people who were sick or sad, and that the two were basically the same thing.

---

There are two left. I've decided to keep them.

Not forever. I'm not building a shrine to legumes. But the freezer is mine now, and I've started filling the space around them. Last week I made split pea, badly, because I don't have her hands or her patience or her unshakable belief that a ham hock solves most problems. I let it cool, ladled it into a quart container, pressed down the lid, and tore off a strip of masking tape.

I stood there with the pen for a long time, trying to think what was worth saying.

*Split pea — Aug 2023 — too thick. Cardinal still fighting the mirror. Missing you.*

Then I put it in the freezer, next to hers, where it will keep.
